But it is solved in other parts of South Africa more or less. It would be solved altogether and for ever, if the principle of equality could be established all round. It is the one state where inequality is the rule which keeps the
rest in a fever	I see it suggested
in some quarters that the policy of Her Majesty's government is one of aggression. I know better than any man that their policy, so far from being one of aggression, has been one of singular patience, and such, I doubt not, it will continue. But it cannot relapse into indifference.
True it is, Mr. Speaker, that the British policy in South Africa has been, a policy of singular patience. Since Majuba, in 1881, the British government have borne and foreborne, and they never made an effort to place a military force in South Africa until rebellion had reared its crest, until two states had given unmistakable signs of an intent to raise the flag of rebellion against British authority. Well, the Bloemfontein conference was held, the negotiations failed and wrongs went on unredressed. Then came the ultimatum to which the Prime Minister has referred this afternoon, issued upon the 9th October, 1899, and 1 think it well, Mr. Speaker, to place the demands of this ultimatum upon record in this House. This ultimatum, in two Instances, spoke of the independence of the Transvaal republic being threatened. The ultimatum was as follows :
That all points of mutual difference shall be regulated by the friendly course of arbitration, or by whatever amicable way may be agreed upon by this government with Her Majesty's government.
That the troops on the borders of this republic shall be instantly withdrawn.
That all reinforcements of troops which have arrived in South Africa since June 1, 1899, shall be removed to the sea coast, with an assurance that they will be removed from South Africa within a reasonable time, to be agreed upon with this government, and with a mutual assurance and guarantee on the part of this government that no attack upon or hostilities against any portion of the possessions of the British government shall be made by the republic during further negotiations within a period of time to be subsequently agreed upon between the governments, and this government will, on compliance therewith, be prepared to withdraw the armed burghers of this republic from the borders.
That Her Majesty's troops which are now on the high seas shall not be landed in any port of South Africa.
Well, this is a refreshing piece of assurance, a refreshing piece of impudence. One 43
wonders, in the light of subsequent events, what the burghers of the Transvaal and what Mr. Beitz, the Secretary of State, who penned this ultimatum, imagined the feelings of the British government would be- the troops on the borders of the republic to be instantly withdrawn, troops that had been landed since June 1st, of that year to be sent to the sea coast, troops then on their way from Great Britain to South Africa to be diverted from their destination and sent somewhere else. Why, the most powerful nation of Europe, the greatest empire in the world, would not have ventured to dictate an ultimatum of that character to a first or even a second rate power. This ultimatum left no doubt-if doubt had previously existed-of the tendency and the trend of events and the inevitable struggle that was at hand. And immediately upon the issuing of this ultimatum, the Orange Free State wheeled into line. There was concerted action between the Orange Free State and the Transvaal. It was perfectly well understood that the two were to act in concert, and the sympathy of a very large portion of the Dutch inhabitants of Cape Town were in the same direction. Then came the invasion of Natal following almost immediately by the investment of Ladysmith, Kimberley and Mafeking, and the annexation, as the right hon. the First Minister told us this afternoon, of British territory to the Orange Free State. Then came the flight of the refugees, which was characterized by the infliction of great cruelty and barbarity on the part of the Dutch inhabitants of the Transvaal. Here is one little incident mentioned in the work of Mr. Bell:
The cause of the assaults was that the refugees left the trucks or carriages for the purpose of obtaining sustenance on their long and painful journey. For this they were lashed and assaulted by armed Boers of the Free State, although they offered no provocation, and although no state of war existed between the republics and Great Britain. Women in the crowded trucks, in some, instances, gave birth to children, passengers were spat upon, and in one case, of which I have particulars, the father of a thirsty child was beaten back to the train, only to witness the death of his child from thirst, although water was obtainable at the station at which he endeavoured to procure it.
This is a specimen among many that might be cited of the atrocities that were perpetrated by these men, on whom the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) expends his sympathies, the Boers of South Africa.
The issue, whatever the hon. member for Labelle may believe, of this war. has been from the outset plain and clearly defined. The issue has been and is to-day : Is South Africa to be Dutch or British ? That is the issue, and there is no middle ground between these two conditions. South Africa must be the one or the other. If we insist upon staying in that country, it will be British, but if my hon. friend from Labelle has his way, It

A Dominion of South Africa will be the realization, in all probability, of the near future, a dominion, where these states will be confederated provinces, where this Boer population, now discordant and hostile, will settle down into peaceful aud loyal citizens. We have already in history one instance of the absorption of a Dutch colony-the colony of New Amsterdam forming now the state of New York. This colony was conquered by England. The same bitter hostility existed among the New Amsterdam Dutch that exist to-day in the Transvaal and Orange Free State, but this population became assimilated with the Anglo-Saxon and merged with the other population of the United States. The Knickerbocker element in New York is distinct to-day to some extent from the other elements, but it is as thoroughly loyal, thoroughly Americanized, thoroughly English-speaking in the broad sense -as any element in the United States, and the same results will be produced in the case of the Dutch element in the Gape Colony, the Transvaal and the Orange Free State. It will be one of the great works in which England is engaged to assimilate, to render the different elements of the population homogeneous, to introduce amity and goodwill among them by the influence of British institutions which will give to all these people their rights, under which no one will have the advantage over another, but all will be equal before the law-all British subjects, secure in the possession of their rights and property. These very misguided Afrikanders will in the near future realize the mistake they made in resisting an authority which wjll confer upon them blessings such as they have never enjoyed or even dreamed of in the past.
These contrasts exist to-day between the purposes of those two elements. The Boer leader desires to oppress the British, the British leader desires to grant every human and every natural right to the Boer. I do not need to dwell upon the impertinence of this resolution which professes to instruct England in the proper course for that great nation to pursue in the settlement of a matter with which we really have no direct connection. The effect upon our interests in Canada of our participation in this struggle has been most salutary and beneficial. Canada has secured a recognition from the world at large that she never had before. The world realizes that in this vast region north of the United States there is growing up a nation ; the world realizes that this country now has a population which possesses energy and courage and devotion to the interests of the empire, and is worthy of respect and worthy of consideration. The cost of sending the contingents from Canada to South Africa is infinitely more than recouped to this country by the beneficial influences which are the result of that action, and which will redound in so
many ways to the credit and to the advantage of the Dominion. Our interest in this matter is a direct one. It is not a matter of pure sentiment, although sentiment had much to do with it, but our material interests are of a character to have rendered the participation of Canada in this struggle a natural thing to do. As I have said, England is our great market. We can only maintain that market by maintaining ttie power and the prestige and the prosperity of the empire that affords it. We have been driven to seek that market. We have been driven from the markets of the United States. We market torday $70,000,000 worth of farm products in Britain out of a total of $80,000,000 that we produce. We cannot afford to lose that market, and it is a matter of the most vital importance to Canada that England and all her interests shall be maintained inviolate. And so it goes beyond the sphere of sentiment and comes down to the sphere of actual material interests, when we take our position as a portion of the British Empire and are prepared to bear our share of the sacrifices, and of the cost in blood and treasure, if that be necessary, for the defence of those interests. The integrity and the glory of this empire is our individual interest. We have a sentimental interest, but speaking from the low standpoint of material interest alone we cannot afford to see Britain's career in Africa, or in any other quarter of the globe, hampered or made to fail. These, Mr. Speaker, in brief, are some of the thoughts I wish to present to this House in reference to this great question which has been brought up for discussion to-night in the manner in which it has.
In dismissing this question, I wish to refer to a personal matter. My warrant for doing so is an insinuation or direct charge rather, made by the hon. member for La-belle (Mr. Bourassa). I am sorry, Sir, to trouble the House or to take up the time of the House with a matter of such trivial consequences to the country as the one I am about to allude to. and I shall allude to it as briefly as possible. My hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) with an evident animus that did not indicate the possession of the most friendly kind of feelings, referred to the report that has been circulated with regard to an alleged utterance of mine during the late election in a speech made at Delhi, in the north riding of Norfolk. I suppose I need hardly say to members of this House that in the heat of an extempore speech upon the hustings, men sometimes undoubtedly make use of expressions which, if they had time to carefully weigh their words, and had an opportunity afterwards to revise their speech, would appear in a different shape before the public. At times the reporter who is giving a synopsis of the speech may unintentionally convey a false impression or an impression not warranted by the language of the speaker. He may at times misunderstand the speaker. The speaker may in the hurry and

excitement of an extempore speech fail to express in language exactly the idea that he intended to convey. In the speech in question, if I remember correctly, I distinctly made the statement in reply to the chairman, that I disclaimed any intention to cast an aspersion or an insinuation upon the loyalty of my French Canadian fellow-citizens. This House is no doubt aware that I have on different occasions spoken highly of the loyalty of the French Canadians ? I remember upon one occasion referring to their loyalty, when thirteen years after the conquest of Canada an attempt was made at the time of the revolt of the thirteen colonies to detach them from their allegiance to Great Britain, and when that attempt signally failed. The French Canadians then, with only thirteen years experience of British rule, proved steadfast and true in their allegiance to the institutions of England. I have spoken of their loyalty upon other occasions. On the 5th day of March, 1900, in conection with an attack made in this House upon my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) growing out of certain incidents that arose in the riot at Montreal, I referred to this question, and without quoting from that speech, I ask my French Canadian fellow-members to do me the kindness to read the speech which is reported in ' Hansard' of the 5th of March. I state here now that that speech expresses my sentiments and that I stand by the assertions made therein.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, the great importance of maintaining friendly relations between the diverse races in this Dominion. I realize that the man who would do anything to disturb these friendly relations ; the man who would wantonly create bitterness and friction is an enemy of his country. I realize that we must go on together side by side and hand in hand in the development of Canada, if we are to make a success of the experiment of British institutions on this North American continent. Of course I am not of French descent ; I am an Anglo Saxon ; I am a Protestant, and all I ask is to have my own particular views respected and be allowed to entertain them, while I grant equally and fully the same privileges to the man who does not agree with me. We have got to build up our in-stitut'ons upon the broad basis of civil and religious liberty. We cannot make religious tests here, and a few days ago I spoke from this point of view in a manner which will clearly indicate the position I take with regard to religious tests and declarations which are offensive and unfair to any body of Christians, or any sect in the Dominion of Canada or in the British Empire. But, Sir, I say again that in taking this position I surrender no tenet that 1 hold, no principle that I entertain, and I ask no other man to surrender any of his. I repeat that I ask of him to respect my rights under the broad principle of civil and religious liberty, and I

pledge to him that I will endeavour to respect his. So much for that point.
How, Mr. Speaker, with regard to the question as to whether, in the speech referred to, I gave expression to the opinion that it would be a good idea to have a British garrison at Quebec, I say I did express that opinion; and the difficulty arises when there is attributed to me, for the expression of that opinion, the belief that disloyalty in Quebec rendered such a step necessary. It was not upon such a ground that I expressed the opinion that it would be a good thing in the interest of Canada to have a garrison at Quebec. On the contrary, Sir, I believe it would be in the interest of all Canada to have the great strategic position of Canada garrisoned.
Why not Toronto ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. Mr. Tarte).

speechtext: Why not Toronto, or any other place ? Why should it be taken as an imputation on the loyalty of any place that a garrison is stationed there ? Is it any imputation on the loyalty of Halifax that there is a garrison there? Is it any imputation on the loyalty of Yictoria that there is a garrison at Esquimalt ? I would make Quebec the military headquarters of the Dominion ; I would put the arsenal of the country there for the store of arms ; I would make that citadel an impregnable stronghold. I would do it for the purpose of bringing into contact with the French Canadians influences that would have a tendency to make the two races better acquainted with each other-for the purpose of letting the French Canadians see the British flag, mingle with British officers, and enjoy the social relations that would naturally grow out of that circumstance. I go further : I believe in making Quebec-and I hope the Minister of Public Works will pardon me-the great commercial centre of this Dominion ; and I think my hon. friend the premier understands that to be my belief-

Hear, hear.
Mr. CHARLTON

for I once waited
upon him with a delegation for the express purpose of promoting the commercial interests of Quebec. It seems to me absurd to dig a hole in the bottom of Lake St. Peter, when we have a harbour 130 miles further down the river, which can be kept open two or three months longer than the harbour of Montreal, possibly the whole year. Vessels from Port Oolborne can go to Quebec as well as to Montreal to transfer their cargoes to deep-draught ocean steamers.
So, upon commercial, social and political grounds, I am in favour of making the city of Quebec the headquarters of the military system of Canada, and the commercial headquarters of Canada, bringing it great prosperity, running a railway line to James Bay, and. diverting the trade of that

region and of other regions to Quebec by through lines to the interior, and centering at Quebec great resources, great buisness interests, great prosperity, and a great population. What will be the effect of that, in a political sense ? It cannot do otherwise than accelerate that process of assimilation and the creation of that homogeneity and affinity which we all desire, and which must be the precursor of the full exercise of the powers of the Dominion in the line of progress. It always makes me sad to reflect that there are, perhaps, a million people in Quebec who cannot speak the English language, who are deprived of the opportunity to test their powers, who are, deprived of the opoprtunity to make headway in the world, who cannot do justice to themselves because they are not In touch with the race which flas the commercial transactions, the business transactions and the capital.
For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I did give utterance to the opinion that there should be a British garrison in Quebec, for the purpose of bringing into contact with each other, to the extent that a garrison would do so, the two branches of the population. Quebec ! Why, I have love for Quebec, Mr. Speaker. Queenly Quebec, beautiful for situation, with its white hamlets and its green fields, surrounded by its mountains ; Quebec, the impregnable old fortress ; Quebec, the strategic centre of North America, Quebec, the gateway of the north, at the foot of whose citadel-crowned promontory the waters of the great inland fresh water seas and the Atlantic mingle, and from whose harbour there extends westward the shining pathway over which her early explorers and voyagers sought the far west and founded the French posts around in the rear of the English settlements along the Atlantic. Historical Quebec, where one of the great epochs of history was wrought out, and the hand of fate decreed that the course of an empire should be changed. I should not like to contemplate the possibility or the probability of retaining that grand historic spot as a city where there would continue to be ten speaking French to one speaking English-as a city which would not fulfil the destiny which Providence designed for it. I want to see Quebec the great centre of this Dominion, in commerce, in wealth, in activity; one of the great factors in assimilating the two populations whose united efforts, if they do unite, will be so conducive to the prosperity, the wealth and the advancement of Canada.
I trust, Mr. Speaker, that these explanations which I have made with regard to this matter will set at rest the aspersion which has been levelled against me, that I insinuated that we wanted a garrison at Quebec because, forsooth, we wanted to keep a disloyal population overawed and in order.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that under all the
circumstances it would have been just as prudent for me, at the time that speech was made, to have said nothing about a garrison at Quebec; it gave opportunity for misconception. If I were making the speech again, I would no doubt avoid saying anything about it. But, nevertheless, I do not take back water, and I am in favour of putting a garrison at Quebec, centering railroads there, centering business there, and making Quebec a great business and social centre.

Mr. Speaker, I really do not think I should interfere in the little family party that has been going on this afternoon on the other side of the House. We first find the very eloquent and charming member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) introducing, a rather radical resolution. Then, we find the right hon. premier coming on with his silver-tongued oratory, completely setting at nought the arguments of the young member for Labelle; and I must congratulate the right hon. gentleman on the very excellent, patriotic and really loyal speech he made. Then, we find our good friend, the independent member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), coming on to-night, and, I believe, from his conclusion, that the real object of his speech was to square himself for a speech which he delivered on a previous occasion. He says that if he had to do it over again, he would not deliver that speech. I have heard it whispered that that speech won him a very easy election. Inasmuch as it has been referred to, I have a copy of that speech, which I will read to- the House, in order to let the House see whether the speech in question has justly caused this little turmoil or not. It is taken from the Toronto Globe, of October 20, 1900. The hon. gentleman starts out in that pious manner which is characteristic of him, by saying :
God forbid that he should say anything against the French or call their loyalty into question, but he could not be ignorant of the fact that the tri-colour is shown in Quebec a thousand times where the Union Jack is shown once. These people look back with regret to the time when the empire passed from the hands of France to England, and the history of North America was changed, and while he would not abridge one iota the privilege the French Canadian possesses or insinuate aught as to his loyalty, yet he would say that the safety of Canada lay in Anglo-Saxon hands, and realizing that, he felt it would not be improper to have a British garrison stationed in Quebec-

To make it a commercial centre, or perhaps apply the provisions of his Seduction Bill.
Mr. HUGHES (reading)-
-ready at any moment to assert British authority under any circumstances or emergencies that might arise.
Did I hear some one say something about commercial union ?
I said it was to make of Quebec a commercial centre, or perhaps apply the provisions of his Seduction Bill.

I thought it was a commercial union that was spoken of. However, I was glad to hear to-night the right ring from the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), and I was sorry this afternoon to hear the hon. member for Labelle waste his eloquence in the way he did. I thought that he would have presented the other side of the question-because every question has two sides-in a logical manner, and one characteristic of that hon. gentleman on most occasions ; but I think the House will agree with me that little pickings from newspapers here and there, up and down the country, could not be considered argument in any sense. I trust, however, that he will see the error of his ways, and that when another session rolls on we will find him on the floor of the House using his splendid eloquence along the right lines, in building up the British Empire and defending everything noble in the cause of humanity.
Had it not been for one or two statements, I would not have spoken to-night, because a short time ago I spoke in this House, at considerable length, on this question from a historical standpoint. My hon. friend stated that Britain was unable to find recruits for her forces in South Africa, and therefore had to call on the colonies. But surely my hon. friend, who has evidently been reading the papers very assiduously, must have found out in the course of the last few weeks, in the English and Canadian newspapers, items by the score, showing that Great Britain does not know what to do with the number of men who have volunteered to serve in South Africa.
I was very sorry to hear the hon. gentleman this afternoon join in the slanders that have been cast at the British troops in South Africa. He referred to the conduct of British soldiers in insulting women. I was more than pained to hear a member of this House, who should have been inspired by the chivalric instincts characteristic of the race from which he springs, speak the way he did. The city of Ottawa has furnished an instance of how these slanders have arisen and how they have been utilized by the pro-Boer party in England. We have Lieutenant Morrison, an officer in the artillery, of this city, quoted all over the United States and the British Empire as having written certain things slandering the British troops, showing how cruel they have been in their treatment of the Boer women and children. Yet we find that Lieutenant Morrison was misquoted, and when what he did say was put alongside of the garbled version of his utterances, the conduct of those who circulated the slander is clearly shown to the light.
Let me give an instance that came under my own personal notice when in South Africa. One of the officers in command at one of the stations received a letter from a Boer lady, whose husband had been one of

the chief members of the war committee, and was a prisoner. She complained that her house had been broken into the previous evening, and that she had been insulted by two British soldiers. The matter was taken promptly in hand and a patrol visited the place. There was not found the slightest sign of the house having been broken into, and when questioned the woman said that it was not her house, but a neighbour's. Her letter was produced, in which she had alleged that it was her own house, but she pleaded that she had written it in a state of great excitement, and had intended to say it was her neighbour's, a woman by the name of Mrs. Schalkurjk. A visit was made to the neighbour's house, and Mrs. Schalkurjk told the patrol that her only ground for saying her house had been broken into was that two soldiers had stopped there the previous evening, as they rode by, and made some inquiries. These men had never offered the slightest word of insult, yet this woman had the hardihood to write to the officer in charge of the station that her house had been broken into and herself insulted. All these facts are on record, but if that story had been allowed to go uncontradicted it would have afforded campaign material to be utilized by gentlemen of the views of my hon. friend from Labelle.
That hon. gentleman spoke of the failure of the British army in South Africa. Well, I took occasion recently in this House to point out that the rule in war is that one man behind a fortification breast high is equal to eight or ten advancing against him. And when instead, the ordinary fortification on the plain, you have fortified the mountain fastnesses and kopjes, you can quadruple the strength which each defender has against the enemy. The House must not forget also that Great Britain was upwards of 7,000 miles from the scene of hostilities, and had to transport men and materials all that distance. Hon. members must equally bear in mind that the Boers had 95,000 men in the fighting line, and in order to cope against a force of that size, with all the advantages in their favour that the Boers possessed, Great Britain required to have about 500,000 or 600,000 men in the fighting line. But, instead, she had less than
325.000	men. Little disasters did occur, as will occur in any war, but in the history of the world the qualities shown by the British army in South Africa have never been surpassed. I do not pretend that the generalship on all occasions has been good, but there never has been a war yet where it has always been good, and there never will be. But the fighting qualities of the British soldier, and the general success of the British arms, have never been surpassed,- when we consider the difficulties under which the troops laboured.
The hon. gentleman has referred to New Zealand and New South Wales. I like to Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
believe him honest, for I think he intends to be, but he must know as well as any man in Canada that New Zealand has repeatedly sent contingents to Africa, and New South Wales has sent five contingents to fight there.
But no policemen.
New South Wales sent five men to one sent by Canada.
Soldiers, not police.

These policemen whom we are sending are to be in the service of His Majesty, and not in the service of the colonial government, and may be utilized for fighting purposes if necessary.
I take this opportunity of summing up my hon. friend's position. He is always ready to give advice to Great Britain. The other day he wanted to amend the coronation declaration. Then, some years ago, he voted in favour of the motion, asking that home rule be granted to Ireland ; but he accepts the advantages of the British consular service ; he benefits by the guarantee of the British Empire for the Canadian loan in the money markets of the world ; he profits by the advantage to Canada in the guaranteeing of her national debt, and by the expenditure of British capital in the development of this country.
But he, as a French Canadian, and his fellow-countrymen, enjoy under British rule liberties and advantages that they could not have under any other country that ever existed on God's green earth. And yet, while he enjoys the protection of Britain's army and navy throughout the world, he stands in this House and slanders His Majesty's soldiers fighting the battles of the empire in South Africa. And he says we must not fight. That is not the kind of patriot we want. That is the kind of patriot we saw in France at the close of the eighteenth century ; for instance, in Robespierre, one of those gentry who would weep if he trod on the foot of a cat, one of these tenderhearted men who, did not believe in quarrelling, but who preached the doctrines advocated by my hon. friend from Labelle, and who brought France to the position of which the poet speaks when he says :
But France got drunk with blood to vomit crime, And fatal have her saturnalia been To Freedom's cause in every age and clime.
Liberty is not secured or advanced by the doctrines preached by the hon. gentleman this afternoon. I shall not go into the details of the causes of the Boer trek. I spoke of that here the other night. We are told by the hon. gentleman that the Boers trekked from Cape Colony on account of British tyranny. They trekked because Britain freed the slave, because the Wilberforce Act passed in Great Britain had freed the slaves wherever the British flag flew. The
credit of British discovery was not due, as my hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) said it was primarily, to Livingstone, because he had not reached there when this work' was begun by Moffat and other devoted missionaries who had preceded the Boers on the fertile lands beyond the Orange river and the Yaal. It was through the discoveries of these men that the Boers knew that to the north there was pasture land infinitely better than the barren karroo in the southern part of Cape Colony. The Beers trekked to escape British taxation, or rather that they might have the levying of taxes themselves. As one of themselves puts it, the Boer believes in no taxation except that levied by himself on the British and the Kaffirs. They trekked there that they might see no other white man's smoke, and that they might lay the foundation of a Boer republic with Durban as its seaport. And history from that day to this proves that the Boer has never given up his hope of driving the British into the sea. As I pointed out on a previous occasion, the lack of a seaport in South Africa was Britain's weakness there. In 1795 and 1796 no less than 1,500 British merchantmen were captured by French cruisers operating from Mauritius alone, this being made possible by the fact that Britain had no naval base in South Africa. The fact that Britain must have a naval base in that country makes it absolutely necessary that the country in the rear must be friendly ; and for that, if for no other reason, Britain must control the whole of South Africa from the Zambesi to the sea. I fully expected that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bourassa) would enter into the causes of the war. Both the leader of the House and the member for North Norfolk have pointed out the disabilities under which the Outlanders laboured. But there was one reason, chief of ail, to which these hon. gentlemen did not refer. The American war of Independence was in the main an assertion of the principle that there shall not be taxation without representation. That principle was ruthlessly violated in the Transvaal, and that fact alone was sufficient justification for the Outlanders to resist and for Britain to step in to the assistance of her people. There is another point-in 1877, when Britain annexed the country, Kruger could not pay his own taxes. But to-day he is worth more than Her Majesty was at the time of her death. And Kruger's sons and grandsons, as has been aptly said by a prominent Afrikander, possess more power in South Africa than Queen Victoria's sons and grandsons do in Great Britain. Notwithstanding what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bourassa) says in his speech, the last thing that Kruger and his oligarchy wanted was an independent republic. Kruger knew that the moment that the people had a voice in the management of affairs, that moment he and his oligarchy would disappear. Why. in that whole country, there were only 15.-
000	voters-not as many as in one ward in the city of Toronto. Here was the real motive that was at the root of many poor fellows being brought into the war. The agitators held out before them the vision of Kruger's wealth and told them : Let the Boers join us in a republic and you will soon become wealthy out of her mines too. They went to those farmers who were in debt to mortgagees or shopkeepers-nearly all the money being owed to English people-and said to them : Join us in this war and when it is over your debts will be wiped out, for we shall drive the English into the sea. They commandeered the poor people. On every farm there were a number of poor whites.
1	reasoned with some of the women folk of these poor people. I remember one family, three of whose men were slain one morning. Reasoning with the women as to why they had allowed their men to go to war, their answer was something like this : Even in times of peace we are slaves, we have not laid by enough to move us to the next town much less resist these burghers or to take an independent stand against them ; they have the power over us even in times of peace. How much more is their power when martial law is declared ? For. Mr. Speaker, this territory had all been annexed to the Free State or the Transvaal and the condition of these poor people was worse than slavery. There were some Boers who were patriotic, who fought for what they regarded as a principle ; but their patriotism was of the negative kind-they fought rather for hatred of Great Britain than for love of their fellows. I agree with much that has been said with relation to these people. I am sorry that my hon. friend did not do them justice. They are a great people, and when they become civilized, when they come in contact with the people of the world I am perfectly satisfied they will make a great race. History shows them to be descended from the greatest races the world has ever seen, the Huguenots of France and the Dutch-races that resisted tyranny for ages. Yet, as soon as the Huguenots reached South Africa they were persecuted by these very Dutchmen, and were compelled to give up their language and adopt the manners and customs of the Boers. Consider how the Kaffirs are treated by the Boers. A Kaffir dare not. walk upon the sidewalk, but must take the middle of the road. He could not own an acre of land ; he must not carry on a trade in vegetables ; until two vears ago he could not be married legally. More than that, he had to be attached to some baas and wear a bandage on his arm with his number on it. If he did not wear this bandage, he might be arrested and be made a slave of the state. The system has not always worked very creditably, for they really had indirect slavery in the Transvaal. However, I will not go into these details.
Reference has been made here to-night to the reception accorded to the soldiers re-

turning from South Africa. I want to tell the hon. member for Labelle, that the returned soldiers do not look for receptions. The soldiers who went to South Africa realize that they have done their duty, and that is all the reward they look for. No doubt many lion, gentlemen present have read this old adage :
When war's proclaimed, and danger's nigh,
' God and the soldier,' is the cry ;
, When war is over, and wrongs are righted,
God is forgotton and the soldier slighted.
The soldier realizes this, and he looks for no favours. He knows that there are people in any community, especially a community such as this, who oppose soldiering in any form; he knows lie will get no sympathy from them. He knows, moreover, that for every one who went off to the front there were fifty others anxious to go, and these will naturally look with a little jealousy if exceptional favours should be showered upon those returning. As a consequence, if he is a sensible soldier, he will, on coming home, go back to his business, and by respecting himself endeavour to command the respect of the community. I tell my hon. friend from Labelle that lie would do himself credit, he would do credit to the chivalrous race to which he belongs, were he to rise in his place to-night and ask the indulgence of this House while he retracted the foul slander that he has cast upon the British soldier in South Africa for his conduct towards women. I say he would command the respect of this House and of the people of this country also, were he to retract the foul slanders which he has cast upon the soldiers of His Majesty in calling them loyal murderers. I trust my good friend will accept these suggestions and act accordingly. I could quote copious extracts from Afrikanders and Boers to refute the slanders of the.hon. gentleman; because all Boers are not disloyal. Many have been loyal to Britain, and have fought manfully for the British flag in South Africa, and have spoken manfully, and used their efforts in every way to put an end to this unhappy war. But it is not necessary to quote these extracts under the circumstances, inasmuch as the hon. gentleman made no attempt to defend his assertions. I have merely taken this opportunity to reply to the hon. member for Labelle on account of his slandering of British soldiers.

Inasmuch as I have a resolution on the paper which has a bearing upon the question now before the House, I shall content myself with saying only a few words. The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) spoke this afternoon for something over two hours, and although he spoke loudly, it was difficult for me to learn all his sentiments, but I did learn sufficient to convince me that his sentiments are not the same as my own.
Is the House ready for the question ?
I shall not abuse my right to reply.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bourassa) has no right to reply.
Is this not a motion ?
There is no right to reply on a motion in amendment to go into Committee of Supply.
I will submit to your ruling, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, before the question is put, there are one or two words that I would like to address to the House in regard to this motion. I think there is a great deal of point in what my hon. friend (Mr. Robinson, Elgin), who has just spoken, lias brought to the attention of the House. It is that this resolution was very unnecessarily introduced, and that we really have wasted a whole day in this House without any possible benefit, so far as I can see, that can in any way accrue from the introduction of the resolution. I am bound to assume that the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) intended some good by this resolution ; I am bound to assume that, because I have the pleasure of that hon. gentleman's acquaintance, and I have seen nothing of him which would induce me to think that he brought this resolution before the House without some definite aim, but, I am equally bound to say that I cannot, for the life of me, conjecture what idea he had as to any good which could result from the introduction or this resolution. I cannot believe that the hon. gentleman supposed that this resolution would pass the House. A very large portion of the speech he delivered in the House to-day I have heard before, certainly on one occasion, and, I think, on two occasions, in the last parliament. The hon. gentleman obtained, on those occasions, an expression of the opinion of this House, which, I think, should have convinced him that no possible good could result from the introduction of this resolution, and I regret that the ability and talents that we must all concede to that hon. gentleman in a high degree have not been put in this House to a better use than they were put by that hon. gentleman. I say this to my hon. friend without in the slightest degree desiring to be offensive to him, and I assure him that I say these words to him in all possible sincerity and friendship. He dealt with all manner of subjects, from the customs and laws of our
Teutonic ancestors to the causes of Mr. Chauvin's defeat in the province of Quebec, and he dealt with the causes of the decline and fall of the Roman Empire as well as with the position of both political parties in the late election in the province of Quebec. Well, I do not quite see, as the right hon. gentleman who leads the House (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was unable to see, the relevancy of all this to the particular motion which we are invited to pass in this House. And, I would go further
I think the leaders did not like it.

I trust that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bourassa) did not take up the time of the House merely for the purpose of saying something that would be displeasing to both leaders. For my part, 1 am bound to say that a portion of the hon. gentleman's remarks was displeasing to me, not that portion of his remarks which reflected upon the political party which I have the honour to lead in this House, because, 1 intend to let those remarks of my hon. friend pass without a single word ; but, I do regret that the hon. gentleman introduced into his speech certain remarks which seemed to me to invite controversy along certain lines which, I, for one, do not desire to see introduced in this House.
Hear, hear.

The right hon. leader of the House has stated that the speech which was made by the hon. mover of this resolution was irrelevant. I entirely agree with that statement, and I go farther; I say that the resolution itself, so far as the preamble is concerned, is absolutely irrelevant to the conclusion. How does the hon. gentleman invite us to deal with this subject ? He invites us, in .the first place, to bring to the attention of His Majesty that we are not committed to any future participation in the wars and policy of Great Britain. Well, that is a matter as to which I, at once, concede the hon. gentleman is entitled to have his opinion. I find no fault with him because he differs possibly from my opinion in regard to that. He proceeds to say :
That the 'contribution of Canada in the South African war, both in armed help and public expenditure, entitles the Canadian people to express an opinion in the matter.
Well, it may entitle the Canadian people to express an opinion in the matter, but, certainly, it does not entitle the hon. member for Labelle to express an opinion in the matter, because he has from the first to the last held that we should have nothing at all to do with it, and should not be expected to contribute to it.

As long as the contribution was not paid I objected to the payment of it, but the moment our contribution

was made, as well as the contribution of all British citizens, 1 became entitled to express my opinion on the matter as well as any one else, whether I pay willingly or am forced to pay.

I think the hon. gentleman may be regarded as having waived his former position. He is willing to take advantage of the contribution we have made for the purpose of introducing this resolution into parliament. 1 am very glad to know that the hon. gentleman has been converted to that small extent, but the hon. gentleman was not very logical, as the right hon. leader of the House pointed out, because, while he is very desirous of giving advice to the Imperial government, he is not at all dsirous of giving any assistance in the wars of the empire. I think the hon. gentleman was hardly worthy of himself when he suggested, that, no matter what force assailed the empire, we, in Canada, were to stand to one side until the soil of Canada was assailed. Does the hon. gentleman expect that the empire will stand to one side when only the soil of Canada is assailed ? Suppose that such an eventuality should occur, as it may possibly occur, although we all hope and trust it never shall, that the soil of Canada should be assailed by an armed invader, whom we were unable to repel, would the hon. gentleman then think that the remainder of the empire should say : We have nothing at all to do with Canada, we are not assailed, we shall stand to one side ? Unless we are prepared to accept that position, how shall we say. while enjoying as we do all the protection of the British Empire, and the British navy, that we are never to join the forces of the empire unless the soil of Canada is assailed ? I known my hon. friend (Mr. Bou-rassa) has a generous nature, and I trust and believe that when he comes to consider this matter in its true aspect, he will not always adhere to some of the opinions which I have heard him express in this House in regard to it. Let us look at the rest of his resolution. He then proceeds as follows :
This House therefore humbly reminds His Majesty King Edward VII. that the glorious reign of his august mother, Queen Victoria, whose memory shall ever be cherished by Canadians of ail origins and creeds, was inaugurated in bloodshed and rebellion in this part of her dominions; that peace and prosperity were subsequently restored and for ever when Her Majesty's advisers understood, as Lord Grey told in his instructions to Lord Elgin, Governor of Canada, that it was ' neither possible nor desirable to carry on the government of any of the British provinces in North America in opposition to the opinions of its inhabitants;' that since that time, Her Majesty has found in no portion of her empire a more faithful, devoted and contented people than her French Canadian subjects.
Possibly I would be inclined to say that my hon. friend might have simply used,
with regard to that, the word ' Canadian subjects.' I tbink that would have expressed his meaning just as well, and would have been equally true.

I would not like to interrupt the hon. gentleman too frequently, but I may be allowed to state that my intention was to point out that in countries where there are different races, the government of these races could not be conducted unless by the application of those principles which I contend are not applied in South Africa. Therefore, I wish to point out that the non-British population of this country have come to love the British flag on account of the application of these principles.

I must remind my hon. friend that it was not French Canadians alone who were in rebellion in 1837, because in the province of Ontario English Canadians, if I may so designate them, were in rebellion also. Therefore, the hon. gentleman's views as expressed in this resolution have no more application to the French Canadians than they have to the inhabitants of the province of Ontario, who were endeavouring in the same way to obtain redress of the grievances under which they believed they were then labouring. But I desire to ask the hon. gentleman: what has all this historical reference to wrongs which were suffered in Canada in 1837 to do with the invasion of British territory by the Boers-because my hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) proceeds afterwards to say in his resolution : therefore, we are to resolve so and so. Two hostile states, the Orange Free State and the Transvaal invaded British territory in South Africa, and Britain used force to repel them. They not only invaded British territory, but it is beyond doubt that they invaded British territory for the purpose of making that territory their own. I will not ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bourassa) to take my statement with regard to that, but I will ask him to accept the statement of the Boers themselves and here is their own language ; the language of the Boer Peace Committee, addressed to the people of Cape Colony, and reported in the London Times of the 9th of January last. Referring to the misery and desolation that had been brought about by the war, they say this :
All this misery is caused by a small and obstinate minority who will not bow to the inevitable and who make the majority suffer. Any encouragement to the men still on commando to continue the hopeless struggle can only injure us and cause us further misery.
I call the attention of my hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) to what follows :
We have done our best and fought to get Africa under one flag, and we have lost.
There is the Boers' statement that this war was precipitated for the purpose of bringing all the British possessions in South

Africa under the Boer flag. Does my hon. friend suggest, in view of that, that when that invasion has been repelled, when (as has been pointed out by the right hon. the Prime Minister), British territory has been declared to have been annexed to these hostile states ; does my hon. friend suggest that we are to hold our hand and leave the British possessions in South Africa still menaced by the very same danger which has been present during the past ten years, and which has recently assailed them. This letter continues as follows Let there be no mistake about this. England has spent millions and sacrificed thousands of lives, and no reasonable being can believe for one moment that she will now give up the fruits of victory. It is, therefore, a duty for us, her beaten foe, to accept the terms offered by our conqueror. . . . England has definitely announced that she will not restore the independence of the two republics. Let us, in the interests of lasting peace in South Africa, accept this announcement as final, and let us work for conciliation on that basis. There is a suggestion in these words which my hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) might well have taken to heart before he ventured to make the speech which he has made in the House this afternoon, and before he ventured to introduce this resolution. For my part I do not think that the speech of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bourassa) really required any answer in this House. I would have been content to vote on the question, upon the basis that the hon. gentleman had confuted himself. I do not think that the question of the causes of the war comes properly under discussion at this present time, and while I do not say that it was not advisable for the right hon. the Prime Minister to go into that, yet I do say that it was not necessary. Under the circumstances which now exist in South Africa ; in view of the fact that the Boers themselves admit that conquest of British territory was the object of the war they began ; in view of the fact that the great majority of the Boers admit that they are beaten ; in view of the fact they they admit (as they do admit in those letters) that the terms which are offered to them by England are fair terms-it was not necessary to introduce such a resolution in this House at all. I venture to think that we have work to do in this parliament at this session which is more worthy of our attention than matters of this kind. It has been our hope and our expectation that we should finish the business of this session within some measurable time, and for my part I say in all sincerity that I have endeavoured to expedite the business in this House, and I intend to do so in future. But if we are to take up a day or two days at a time for the purpose of discussing matters which are of purely Imperial concern, it seems to me that we are going to have only a very moderate amount of time to devote to subjects that really do concern this par-	liament. I am prepared to vote against this resolution, and I would have been prepared to vote against it even if I had not heard the very able and eloquent speech which the right hon. the leader of the government delivered to this House, as well as the speeches of the other hon. gentlemen who followed him. I have seen articles in some newspapers, in which it was stated that there were practically no schools located among the Doukhobors, and I would like to know what portion of this vote is for that purpose.

cation in the organized territories is carried on by the North-west government. They are required to look after the education of the people out of their subsidy.
Grant for schools, clerical assistance,
printing, &c	 $332,979

Under this item perhaps the hon. minister can give us some information with reference to the schools established by the territorial government. I am of opinion that something ought to be done in some way for the education of the Doukhobors. They ought not to be allowed to live in communities by themselves without some provision being made for their education.

The North-west government have had for years past a school Act under which they organize school districts just as is done in other portions of the western country; and they give a special grant to each school district in proportion to the amount of work done. I do not know that I have any special information with regard to the arrangements they are making for school districts amongst the foreign settlers; but I can give the hon. gentleman the statement made by the North-west government with regard to education in applying for this grant. During the year just closed they have expended in all 8187,591. Petitions were received during the year for the erection of ninety-nine new school districts, of which forty-nine have been erected and fifty are in process of construction. The heavy immigration of the past two or three years causes a rapid increase in the expenditure on schools.
In discussing the estimates with the members of the North-west government, they urged very specially upon me during the last couple of years the necessity for an increase in their grant on account of the increased amount of educational work to be done in the new settlements. Last year an increase was given, but in this vote there is no increase. My impression, however, is that next session we will have to ask an increase.
Are the children taught the English language ?
No other language is taught.
I would like to have a statement from the hon. gentleman as to the erection of the portion of the Territories into a province. Is that likely to happen after the census is made ?

A deputation consisting of two members of the North-west government, Mr. Haultain and Mr. Ross, were in Ottawa some time ago on other business, and took the opportunity of discussing this question. I may
say that while during the last three or four years they have uot addressed any official communication to the government, yet from time to time they have discussed with myself and my colleagues the question of giving the Territories provincial status, and lately they handed us a memorandum on that subject. We have not officially replied to that memorandum as yet, but ex. pect to do so shortly. This is a matter, of course, requiring serious consideration, but I may say in a general way that I am of the opinion that it will have to be dealt with in the very near future. The people of the Territories are as capable of self government as any other people in Canada, and have shown their fitness by the admirable manner in which they have carried on their present administration. Of course the financial question is a serious one. The subsidy required for the Territories in the course of a few years would have to be greatly increased, and there is the question of the control of public lands and matters of that kind which would have to be settled.
Perhaps the hon. member for Selkirk, who knows a good deal about school matters among the Doukhobors, would favour us with his views.

I do not think that any schools receiving assistance are yet established among the Doukhobors. In some of the outlying villages they attend some of the schools that were established before they arrived; and there are one or two private schools' started by the Society of Friends of Ontario. Some provision should be made with the government of the Territories for the establishment of schools among those colonists, and I think there should be a condition imposed on this vote providing that the North-west government should assist those foreigners in the matter of education as they do English settlers. Any one who has been up there will understand the situation. In two or three months there will come into a district sufficient children to start a new school, and in some cases to start three or four schools, and yet in such cases these people have had to do without schools for two or three years. I have known of one family which came out from Ireland and seriously contemplated returning just because of this lack of schooling facilities. There is no doubt that with the increased immigration, the government of the Territories will not be able to provide adequate schooling facilities unless it gets a larger grant.

speechtext: What is the reason of the increase of $25,000 ?

Will the hon. minister state the policy of the government as to the issue of liquor permits in the Yukon ?

I laid on the Table of the House the other day an order in council providing regulations for the introduction of liquor into the Yukon. Under that order, provision is made for the issue of wholesale licenses an the territory, and permits may be granted to the holders of wholesale licenses but not to any others.
Is the practice to be discontinued that has heretofore existed of issuing permits from the department for parties to take liquor in ?
That has been abolished by the order in council to which I have just referred.

Is it to be the rule in future that, on application being made, wholesale licenses will be issued to the parties for the sale of liquor ? And if these are wholesale licenses, what conditions are made with regard to the retail sale of liquor ?
No permission is given to the retailers to import. They buy from the wholesalers. The holder of a wholesale license may, on application, get a permit.
Do we understand that there will be indiscriminate sale by retail, and that all that will be necessary will be for a party to go to a wholesaler and purchase from him and sell ?
The local council have a liquor license ordinance, under which they issue retail licenses, just as is done in any of the provinces, and parties holding these licenses will have the right to sell.

Is it necessary to the issue of a retail license that there should be a petition from the inhabitants of the locality, as in the case of the province of Ontario, Nova Scotia and perhaps, some others ? Or is It issued merely on applica- ' tion from the party who desires to sell ?

Speaking from recollection, I do not know that there is any provision in the liquor licenses ordinance for a petition from the ratepayers. My hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) will see that the conditions are not the same as in an older place, and that a petition there would not be the same safeguard that it would be here.

Quite so, but I wanted to ascertain what safeguards there are with regard to the character of the person to whom a license is given, the manner In which he is likely to conduct his establishment and his observance of the laws generally. Does the council pass upon these matters without evidence of some sort, or do they make an inquiry, or do they depend upon their own knowledge ?

Provision is made for inspection by an officer appointed for that purpose, and on that a license is granted. That is my recollection of the liquor license ordinance, though I have not read it for something like a year.
Is there any restriction as to the number of licenses granted in a particular district ?
I do not recollect at the moment, but the ordinance wias laid upon the Table of the House last session in pursuance of the statute in that regard.

Mr. LaRIVIERE. I made an inquiry the other day from the minister with regard to a survey that is required in the south eastern portion of Manitoba. We have a railway there which has been partly built and which is attracting the attention of the public, running from Winnipeg in a south-easterly direction. There is a large tract of land there that is still unsurveyed, while there are a large number of settlers who are seeking to settle upon these lands, but who cannot locate them for want of a survey. In fact, I believe the whole of that district east of the Red river, and between the river and the Lake of the Woods should be surveyed. It will all now be available for settlement, and it is only natural that when the settlers come into these districts they should be able to locate their lands. I hope that orders will be given to have all that part of the province surveyed before another season.

In -the list of surveys provided for under this vote I have provision made for one part of that country. We have also a miscellaneous vote for unforeseen requirements to the extent of $18,000. I am quite satisfied that we shall be able, with the money which we have asked parliament to vote, to provide for the surveys to which my hon. friend (Mr. LaRiviere) refers. Our object in dealing with the surveys as we do is to keep ahead of settlement. We cannot at all undertake the policy of a systematic survey of the whole country. We get the best information we can and send surveyors to those parts of -the country into which settlers are going and in which, therefore, surveys are required. Our effort is to keep ahead of settlement.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. I am sorry to say the hon. gentleman has not kept ahead of settlement in this case.

In some cases, we have not been able to do so ; but if my hon. friend will call my attention by letter to any particular part of the country where surveys are required for settlement, I think we can provide for the work that is necessary.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. It is along the Canadian

lars of any case, I will be happy to do what he says.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. I have communicated with the officials of the hon. gentleman's department, and the correspondence is there.
I do not care to divulge the facts before the House, but an official of the department informs me that this man has been paid in full, though he has not paid the men he had employed.

I regret the minister has not seen fit to put in a larger amount for these surveys. There were 8,000 homesteads taken last year, and suppose there are 40 homesteads in a township, 200 townships would require to be surveyed. I understand a surveying party can do in a season about five townships, consequently, they are not going to be able to keep up with the requirements of the people coming into the country. In my opinion, within two years there will be no surveyed lands ready for occupation, because, as the member for Provencher (Mr. LaRiviere) has stated, not only have new surveys got to be made, but a great many of the old surveys, both east and west of the Red river, and in the North-west Territories, have got to be made over, because the men cannot find the posts, the fires have destroyed them. Even in surveys made only three or four years ago, it is almost impossible to establish the posts. Now, in one township alone there are twenty-two Swedes from the United States who have settled, and I am aware that many of them have built their houses off their own quarter sections. This is a great hardship. I understand last year the department had twelve parties in the field doing survey work upon homestead lands, whereas, to keep pace with the actual homesteaders coming in, even if the number should not be increased, it will require forty parties of surveyors to do five townships each. This ought to be taken into consideration before we reach that particular point that we cannot go any further, because a great many of those townships surveyed, or portions of them, are unfit for settlement. I would like if the minister could see his way clear to increase that amount. I think I drew the attention of the government to it when I was an official.

We had something over twenty parties at work last year, and we are preparing this year to send out thirty-one. I am aware that in the future we shall have to make preparation for more surveys to keep pace with increased emigration.

The hon. gentleman says that these posts were burned out two or three years ago ; why should we not put down iron posts ? Iron posts would be very nearly as cheap, and would not require to be renewed in consequence of fire.
Last year there were 6,680 homestead entries. The report says there were 7,426, but you must deduct from that number 746 that w>ere made in the previous year.

I have not got the report with me, but I think my figures are correct. I have got the figures for the months of January and February of this year, and there is an increase of 40 per cent over last year.
