clerks in the outside service	$74,000
Would the hon. gentleman explain the reason of this increase of $8,500 ?

We have been in the habit, for some time past, when there was a pressure of business, of employing temporary assistance. At present we are adding clerks in the following offices, but they are not permanent : One at Winnipeg, $480 ; one at Calgary, $480 ; one at Edmonton, $360 ; one at Lethbridge, $600, and a forest ranger for southern Manitoba, $900. We have had a system drawn up during the last four years, in consequence of the increase of settlement, under which we have had sub-agents. In order to make entries at the land agencies, settlers would have to travel a considerable distance, and we have inaugurated the practice of appointing sub-agents at points where a good deal of settlement is going on.
We have had the system of requiring the settlers to pay fees to these subland agents. We are abolishing that system and we propose to give the subland agents regular salaries, $300 being the largest salary paid. There are eleven of them altogether, and the total salaries will be $3,000. We have additional clerks to appoint at some of the land offices. There is an additional clerk at Yorkton at a salary of $900, an additional clerk at Red Deer at a salary of $720, an additional clerk ht Regina at a salary of $900, and an additional clerk at Brandon at a salary of $1,200, making altogether $3,720. But $2,500 was provided for these items last year, thus making the net increase only $1,220. Then, increases have been given to the following clerks : Mr. A. J. Fraser, land agent at Lethbridge now, increase $105. He has been in the service for a great many years. Mr. B. H. Humphrys, in the commissioners office at Ottawa and, who has also been in the service for a great many years, will receive an increase of $128.75. Mr. Richard Breen, another official gets $120 Increase. Mr. R. C. Kisbey gets $180 increase, Mr. E. W. Burley $200, Mr. E. Trudel $200. Mr. W. McMillan $200, and Mr. G. A. Hogarth $200. the increases in all amount to $1,333.75. The total of these items. $2,820, $3,000, $1,220 and $1,333.75, is $8,373.75. The salaries in the Dominion lands branch,

although the work is fully twice as much as it was in 1895-6, are not yet as large as they were then. The salaries then amounted to $82,500, whereas last year they amounted to $71,550.55. With these increases they will still not be as much as in 1895-6.
I see there are eleven homestead inspectors. Would the hon. minister explain what the duties and salaries of these officials are ?

The homestead inspectors are a class of officials who are provided for and have always been since the homestead system was introduced under the Dominion Lands Act. Their business is to examine the homesteads of such settlers in respect to the applications which they may make for their patents. When a settler finds that he is in a position to apply for his patent, having fulfilled the settlement duties, he notifies the nearest land office that he is in a position to make his application, and the land agent notifies the homestead inspector. The homestead inspector makes an inspection of the homestead and he has a printed form in which certain information has to be given. He makes his report to the land agent, the land agent makes a report and these reports are forwarded to the commissioner's office where the case is adjudicated upon. If the duties have been performed, the settler gets his patent. These are the principal duties of the homestead inspectors. In addition to that, wherever necessary, they act as forest rangers, taking precautions in regard to fires where the land is timbered. They also make valuations of land where they are required to do so by the department, and they do any additional work which the department may require them to perform. They get $1,200 a year each and actual expenses.
Has there been any increase in the number lately ?
Lately a man who was appointed a forester has also been appointed an inspector. His name is McMillan, and he lives at Treherne.

The reason I asked this question was that from general report a very great number of people are going into that country, and I did not see how the same number of inspectors could be doing so much more work than they have been doing here- * tofore. I thought perhaps there had been an increase in their number. I do not know how many the hon. gentleman had before. They certainly appear to be well paid at $1,200 and expenses.
I think the hon. gentleman will find in that evidence that these homestead inspectors are doing more work than they did formerly.

I would like to ask the hon. Minister of the Interior if Mr. Mr. SIFTON.
J. W. Thompson, homestead inspector of Marquette, the gentleman that the hon. minister induced to resign his position in order to contest Marquette with myself, was reappointed to his office as soon as the election was over, and if the hon. gentleman does not candidly think that he comes within the term of an active political partisan ?

Mr. Thompson was reappointed. I have not under my hand the exact date when he was reappointed, but it was a couple of months after the election. I have no information before me that Mr. Thompson has acted the part of an' offensive partisan since he was appointed, but 1 presume that he acted somewhat as a partisan when he contested Marquette with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche). I hope my hon. friend will not take it as an offence if I express some regret that Mr. Thompson was not more successful.

This is rather an extraordinary attitude that nothing has come to the notice of the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sifton) to indicate partisanship. One of his own servants, a gentleman in the employ of his own department, resigns his seat, contests a constituency, is defeated, and then he is rewarded. A string is p'ut on Mr. Thompson when he goes out in order that he will be able to go back in the event of his defeat. Mr. Thompson had nothing to lose by contesting this constituency, and I want to say to the hon. gentleman that he has set an example that does not contribute much to the public morals of this country. The hon. gentleman has his officials, occupying responsible positions throughout the country and living on the public funds, in training to be candidates for the hon. gentleman when the election comes on. I think there are several hon. gentlemen holding seats in this House who came in under such circumstances, who resigned their positions and who equally had a little rope upon them. I have no hesitation in saying that no more vicious principle could be thought of or adopted than the one which is now being carried on in the hon. gentleman's department. Just let the hon. gentleman picture the case of his own officials who are in daily contact with the people who go into that country and try to imagine the undue influence that a man is able to exercise under such circumstances. To say the least it is scandalous in its character. I say it is scandalous inasmuch as 'it is manifestly unfair and unjust and must detract from anything that one would consider in the light of justice, fairness, or right.
Let the minister look at the other side of the question, and see how it would operate. Why, the heads of officials who did absolutely nothing are falling into the basket every day. All that is necessary is to hatch up a charge against some innocent official,
and his head comes off, and there is not even the pretense of a trial. Yet, the minister (Hon. Mr. Sifton) brings out his own officials in a campaign and he brings them back and takes care of them when they are defeated. There is no defence of any kind for such a proceeding, and before these estimates go through the minister must explain whether it is the policy of the government, and his own policy in particular, to continue that state of affairs. Is he going to lay down the policy that an official may look forward to his promotion because he is the candidate of the minister ? I would like to know whether, under such circumstances, an official will serve his country or will serve his political master. He must serve the latter, and do as he is told, because he is not depending upon the merits of his service, but upon the smiles of his superior. I am bound to say that the Minister of the Interior has not been hardhearted, and that he has rewarded his friends. Does he enunciate to this House that that is to be his policy in the future.

My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) is asking me to enunciate a policy upon a very large question. This particular gentleman was offered the nomination by a party convention and he accepted it and resigned his office. I was at the convention, but I had not the least idea that the gentleman had any intention of being a candidate. If he had I knew nothing about it. When I went to the convention I had not the least idea who was going to be nominated. I have had very little acquaintance with this gentleman, and I am not sure that I ever saw him before the occasion of his nomination. If I did I certainly had no particular acquaintance with him. So far as my knowledge goes, and so far as the knowledge of the department goes, he is a competent officer, and I do not see that the fact that he was a candidate in the election is any reason why he should not be reappointed. I quite agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) that if the department systematically went into the business of appointing candidates it would be objectionable.

I do not think that the minister (Hon. Mr. Sifton) has dealt with this question in the way it should Ibe dealt with. We had an announcement of policy from the right hon. the Prime Minister as far back as 1897, in which he stated that if any public servant of this coutnry desired to be a politician he would give him every opportunity of doing so by dismissing him. The doctrine which the right hon. gentleman enunciated then is particularly applicable to this case. The Minister of the Interior says there is no reason for not appointing this official because he was a candidate at an election. That is not the point raised by my hon. friend from Both well (Mr. Clancy). What 44
he denounces is the vicious principle of giving an opportunity to a public servant to resign his position for the purpose of being a candidate for one political party or the other, with the understanding that he will be appointed again if he is unsuccessful.
There was no understanding of that kind directly or indirectly.

That may be, but I have a pretty strong opinion that this gentleman felt sure in his own mind that if he were unsuccessful he would be appointed again. At all events, it is not a good precedent to lay down, and the thing has a very suspicious look in the face of it. We have had many criticisms of offensive partisanship, made by hon. gentlemen opposite. Postmasters getting a salary of $50 or $60 a year have been dismissed by this government because they attended political meetings or something of that kind. For my part I never favoured any such action by one government or the other, because I think a man who gets $50 a year for discharging duties of that kind might very well take such part in public affairs as he thought fit. But the policy of this government has been to turn these men out of office for what they call political partisanship. The pretention of gentlemen opposite is that it is unpleasant to the feelings of Liberals that the man who gives them their mail in the post office should be a man who takes an active interest in public affairs. How much more is that applicable to cases of this kind ? Take a public servant performing the duties referred to in this case, and he may be using his office for three or four years, looking forward to a candidature, while the public, whether of one party or the other, are entitled to the services of that man without any bias. Are they likely to get his services without bias, if that official is looking forward to be a candidate with the exjjressed or applied understanding, or if you like confidence, that if he be unsuccessful he shall stand a good chance of retaining his office 7 The Minister of the Interior might very well act upon the principle which his leader has laid down : that if any public servant in this country desires to be a politician he shall be placed in a position to devote the whole of his time to that particular business. That principle would not justify the minister in reappointing an unsuccessful candidate to this position.

The peculiar feature about this is that Mr. Cox, the predecessor of Mr. Thompson as homestead inspector, was dismissed because it was said he was an offensive political partisan, and the only thing Mr. Cox did-and he was a very successful and experienced



officer-was to write a letter to one of my committee stating tliat lie was going into the Dauphin district, and that if he while there could do anything on the quiet to assist my candidature, so long as it did not leaye him open to the imputation of being a partisan, he would do so. He wrote in words to that effect. This letter was stolen out of the office of one of my committee men, and it was sent to the Minister of the Interior, and, as the minister admitted on the floor of this House, Mr Cox was dismissed on the strength of that. There was no other charge against Mr. Cox. The minister (Hon. Mr. Sifton) admitted he was a first rate officer. No investigation was held. Mr. Cox offered to do something, but the letter was not even replied to. Mr. Cox did not lift his hand in my interest, but in this letter he showed his favour towards me, and therefore, he was considered by the government an active and offensive partisan, and his position was given to Mr. Thompson. Every person who lives in the town with Mr. Thompson, Liberals as well as Conservatives, know that there never is an election held, whether provincial or Dominion, without Mr. Thompson being one of the most active workers in the Liberal ranks. I told the acting minister last session that I could give him the name of a homestead inspector, if he wished, who had been most active in the last provincial election. Mr. Thompson has always been told off to look after the Scandinavian vote located some twenty miles north of the town in which he resides. He was sent up to look after that, and did look after it, while homestead inspector, one year ago last fall, at the time Of the local election, and he openly stated that if there was a change in the Dominion government, he wmuld not wait to be dismissed, but would resign ; he did not make any bones about it. Still, he can do all this and not be considered an offensive partisan. I presume the Minister of the Interior attaches the same meaning to that term that exAttorney General Cameron did in the local legislature, when accused of keeping in the government employ Mr. McDonnell, a member of this House, and an offensive partisan. Mr. Cameron's reply was : 'He was not *offensive to us.' So, I presume the Minister of the Interior discriminates according to the particular party this man is offensive to. As I stated before, I would not bring this case up if it were the only one. Mr. Jerome, one of the hon. gentleman's forest rangers, was allowed to resign his position and run as a candidate for the local legislature. He was successful, and yet got his position back, and he is a member of the local legislature to-day. Is he not an offensive political partisan ? This homestead inspector will be using his position as a lever for getting votes for himself at the next election. I do not object to nis being a can-
didate, because there is no other gentleman I would prefer to have as an opponent.

Surely the Minister of the Interior does not propose to sit silent in the face of a charge so grave-that he goes to a public nomination meeting by accident, that he did not know this gentleman, but that by his presence he gave his sanction to one of his own officials being a candidate. Yet, the hon. gentleman sees no wrong in it, and does not think it worth while to make a statement to this committee about it. It seems to me one of the most appalling things I ever heard of. The hon. gentleman cannot laugh this matter away. If he found his political opponents taking a course of that kind, there is no gentleman who would put more energy and heat into his protest than the hon. gentleman, and very properly too. My hon. friend cites a case of a gentleman being dismissed because he wrote a letter expressing his strong sympathy, and declaring what he would do under certain circumstances. The circumstances never arose, no proof was given that he ever acted, and yet he was dismissed. What followed ? The very gentleman who dismissed _ him puts up one of his own officials, who' was at that time, as the leader of the opposition stated, paving the way for his own election, to be a candidate. No official need hereafter ask permission to run, because, from what has been stated to-night, we can see that it is the policy of the hon. gentleman to allow his officials to do that. I would again ask the hon. gentleman to say whether he disapproves of the candidature of Mr. Thompson, and whether he proposes in future to permit actions of that kind ? I think that is a fair question to ask, and the committee has a right to have a straightforward, unequivocal answer from the hon. gentleman.
I do not see that the hon. gentleman or any one else could prevent a government official resigning and running as a candidate for parliament. That is what the hon. gentleman is finding fault with.
No, I am finding fault with the hon. gentleman appointing him afterwards.

I do not see why he should not be appointed afterwards. If the leader of the opposition had said that I had gone to this man beforehand and asked him to be a candidate, and promised him, if defeated, he would be reappointed, there is no question that that would have been a very reprehensible transaction. I said to the hon. leader of the opposition that there was no understanding between Mr. Thompson and myself, directly or indirectly, in any shape or form ; and that Mr. Thompson had not the least reason to believe, from anything said by me or by my authority, or from
anything said by any pex'son on my behall' or on behalf of the government, that he would be reappointed. When he made his application to be reappointed, he stood in the same position as any other applicant. He might or might not have been appointed. If he had not been appointed, there would have been no grievance against me.
Did the hon. gentleman appoint any one In his place while he was away during those two months ?

No, one of the officers of the staff went up and discharged his duties. Of course, I see the point my hon. friend desires to make, which is, that the fact that there was no permanent appointment made was due to my wish to keep the office open for Mr. Thompson. There was no idea of that kind in my mind, and no understanding of any kind that if he was defeated he would be reappointed. Mr. Thompson was offered the nomination and accepted it. When he made application for the position again, I appointed him. I had no obligation to do so.

How long after the election was it before Mr. Thompson was reappointed ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
About two months, I think.

How long before the election did he resign ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
He resigned on the same day he was nomi-ated.

How long was that before the election took place ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
The convention was on September 3.
Mr.	ROCHE (Marquette).	When Mr. Thompson was nominated, was the position promised to any other person ?The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
No.

When the position was vacant, were there any other applicants for it besides Mr. Thompson 1
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
I cannot say positively, but I think I shall be safe in saying that there were a large number.

The hon. gentleman did not touch on the other portion of the partisanship which I refer to, that is, the part he took in the provincial election.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
I never heard of it. I was in that part of the country and took an active part in the provincial election, but never heard of Mr. Thompson doing so.
44*

Was there not any one of those numerous applicants capable of filling the position 1 There were a great many applicants after Mr. Thompson resigned and his resignation covered a period of two months before the election. Was none of these applicants capable of taking his place 1

Speaking in a general way, thes'e was a number of applications. I do not remember the names of any of the applicants, but I recollect receiving a great many letters from different people. At the time in British Columbia a couple of elections took place after the general election, and I went out to take part in those elections. As soon as I got back and learnt the details, the appointment was made. There were no delays but those which occurred in the natural order of things.
It was remarkably fortunate for Mr. Thompson that the hon. gentleman was so busy during these two months that he was not able to make the appointment.
I am afraid my hon. friend is skeptical.

Not at all. I am accepting his word and am simply mentioning how extremely fortunate it was for Mr. Thompson that the hon. gentleman happened to be so much engaged during these two months. I have no doubt that Mr. Thompson will always select an occasion of that kind when he again decides to resign, an occasion when the hon. gentleman will be too much engaged to deal with the numerous applicants for the position, and Mr. Thompson will thus be amply safeguarded. And when the matter does come up before the hon. gentleman afterwards, Mr. Thompson will have had his election matters disposed of and his name will be at the head of the list. There will, of course, be no understanding expressed or implied, but without any such understanding Mr. Thompson will always be moderately safe. On that account, I can rejoice on Mr. Thompson's behalf that things will be made smooth for him without any understanding expressed or implied.

Such actions as those will make every official in the North-west an active politician, because if he is not elected he will be sure to getting back his office. It is a very wrong thing to do, and I am very sorry that this government should have done such a thing.
Did this man receive any remuneration for any portion of his time after his resignation ?
No.

There is another matter I would like to bring to the attention of the hon. gentleman. The land agent at Minnedosa is an over-worked official. He had an assistant, Mr. Jarvis, who was a very faithful official and occupied the position about nine years. In the Northwest rebellion he met with an accident which entitled him to an annuity from the government. There was no charge of any kind ever made against him, but he was dismissed without cause, and his dismissal was justified by the hon. gentleman on the ground of economy. Yet, strange to say, the land office at Dauphin, the work of which Was largely done through the Minnedosa office by Mr. Jarvis, required a new man, and instead of removing Mr. Jarvis to the Dauphin office the hon. minister appointed a green hand, from the same town, The treatment of Mr. Jarvis was certainly not fair. If he Was not required in Minnedosa he should have been utilized at Dauphin.
When was he removed 7
In 1897, just when a new man was required in Dauphin.
The appointment at Dauphin was some time after that.

Mr. Hogarth was sent to Dauphin just about the time Mr. Jarvis was dismissed. Mr. Jarvis certainly should have been taken on at Dauphin instead of a new man who knew nothing about the business. Mr. Fletcher, the present land agent, has to get help from Winnipeg at the end of each month. Mr. Stevenson has admitted that Mr. Fletcher has too much to do and on more than one occasion' said he would report it to the department. Mr. Thompson, the homestead inspector, has frequently to be taken from his regular duties and placed in this office to assist Mr. Fletcher, and Mr. Fletcher should be given permanent help.

It may appear strange that one coming so far from the east should inquire into what is going on in the Northwest, but a friend of mine from Prince Edward Island went to the North-west some seventeen years ago and was appointed inspector of homesteads. He worked under the government for a number of years until the present administration came into power. He was a Frenchman, John J. Arsenault, a most capable man, and was dismissed without cause and without any investigation. I would ask the hon. minister to deal with him fairly and not have his head go Into the basket without an opportunity of being heard.
The case of Mr. Arsenault is one I happened to be personally acquainted with. I do not think the hon. gentleman or anybody else

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: could complain of his dismissal. He had practically been the election agent of the Conservative party in the part of the country where he lived for some years before his dismissal, and I do not think that his own political friends expected the government to retain his services.
What was the date of the resignation by the hon. member for Selkirk of the position he held prior to his election and the date of the appointment of a successor ?
I do not remember the exact date. It was about the time he was nominated, and his successor was appointed a month ago.
Then his resignation was in at the time of the official nomination or a week prior to the 7th of November 7

I was nominated on the 25th December. I had not seen the Minister of the Interior for six months, nor had I any letter from him when I ran for Selkirk. I was appointed in 1897, and was mayor of Winnipeg, and had been aider-man a number of years, and was requested to be mayor the following year. I had a salary of $1,200 which I resigned. During the entire time I occupied tne position of commissioner of immigration-you will pardon my referring to it to-night, but I do so because it has been referred to by one or two members-during the three years that I occupied that position, not a Conservative in Manitoba or the Territories would venture to say that I took any part in politics. At a meeting of the whole board of trade, with over 400 citizens of Winnipeg present, Mr. A. M. Nanton and Mr. E. L. Drewry respectively, formerly president and vice-president of the Conservative Association-the deputy minister was present and will recollect it, and the papers of that time will bear out what I say-stated that I have never taken any part in politics while I held that office. And let it be noted that while I was in office I did not work under the civil service rule. It was not a case of going to the office at ten o'clock and quitting at half-past four. I was at my office generally at 8.30 in the morning, and I was there until six o'clock in the afternoon ; four out of the seven days of the week I was there in the evenings until ten o'clock; and we never had Saturday afternoons. The office of the commissioner is open every Saturday afternoon, and five or six of the staff are there for half the day on Sunday. It was not my intention when I accepted that office to remain for ever a civil servant. I had ambitions ; and when I was offered a county I accepted it. I did not know, twenty-four hours before, that I should be nominated. After I was nominated, my work being behind, I went to the office of the commissioner and remained
there for the following week or ten days,
X think that my resignation took place on the 1st of October. I asked the deputy minister to credit me with three weeks holidays for each of the four years I had been a civil servant, and allow me salary for that time. He refused. I said to him : Why not allow me, then, for the extra hours that I have put In? But he would not do it.
I do not think it any disgrace to be a civil servant, if one is a conscientious one, as are many in Winnipeg and the Territories. In that immigration hall, in the office to which I was attached, 95 per cent of the employees are as conscientious people as you could put into office.
Who said they were not ?

Well, reflections have been cast. If I, as a civil servant, earn fairly every dollar paid me by the government; and I say that I will retire and run for the Commons or for the local legislature, surely that is all right. And suppose I run and lose, and there is no blot on my record in any way, is it wrong for the minister to appoint me to another office ? If there is anything wrong in that, I would like to know it. For my part, as I see it at present, I do not know what there can be wrong in it, supposing, of course, that while a civil servant, I did not use my position in any way to advance my own political Interest.

I am not reflecting on the hon. gentleman, and simply asked the question to know the circumstances of his resignation. First impressions are always lasting, and I think the impression the hon. gentleman has shown as to the chances or prospects of returning to a position in the event of defeat must certainly have been in his mind at the time for his resignation, and, no doubt, there were facts to bear out that impression.

I may tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) that if I accepted any position or had it been offered to me I did not think that it would be the same position. If the hon. gentleman were as tired of a position as I was of that, he would not accept reappointment. When you handle from 25,000 to 40,000 people a year 8,000 or 10,000 of whom cannot speak English, you get pretty tired of it.

We have had splendid exhibitions of innocence. The minister is innocent, the officials are innocent. An hon. gentleman has declared that he resigned his position without the knowledge of his superior, but thought that if he failed in gratifying his ambition to become a member of the House he might be given a position again. I do not blame the officials who
acted on that view, because they understood, without being told, just what the minister would do. I would like to know whether, supposing a Conservative official, one appointed under the late government, had thought fit to accept a nomination, and had been defeated, no matter how good an official he had been, he would have been appointed. The Minister of the Interior, I venture to say would not have consented to his resigning his position to allow him to be alternately an official in the department and a candidate in an electoral contest. I do not wish to misrepresent the Minister of the Interior. It is well that we should have his view embalmed in ' Hansard,' to use an expression of a former member of this House. He declared in most unmistakable terms that had he been a consenting party to Mr. Thompson's resignation and to his candidacy for election, and had he then appointed him after his defeat, he would have been guilty of a most reprehensible act. What, then, would be the difference in case be had found one of his officials nominated as a party candidate and had neither protested nor disapproved, or had written a letter declaring his full approval of that gentleman becoming a candidate, and then, after his defeat appointing him to another ? Was not this merely carrying on a sort of pantomime ? He did not make the arrangements in words, but acted it. Will any one say that Mr. Thompson did not understand that if he were defeated he would be reappointed ? And in this have we not a state of things that is far from creditable. I have not reflected upon those gentlemen who were formerly officials. If hon. gentlemen opposite wish to find shelter behind such a plea, they must set up that shelter themselves, for no one has alleged anything against these former officials. At the same time, I have not deprived myself, should the occasion arise, to consider the question, and to express my views as to whether these gentlemen were good officials or not.
But at this stage no such allegation has been made. The allegation has been made of unseemly conduct on the part of the government. I do not blame the hon. gentlemen who took advantage of it. They had the assent of their minister, and the minister to-day has made a statement that 1 think is a very alarming one. The hon. gentleman has been accused of permitting his officials to become candidates. Before they became candidates they must certainly have had the consent of the minister. I repeat that the minister might just as well have written a letter calling him into his office and saying to him: You may become a candidate, and if you are defeated, just come back to me and you will have your office again. I am glad the hon. gentleman has put himself on record, and the country will judge accordingly :

That consists of tbe following items : First, there are nine homestead inspectors and five forest rangers continually employed, and to provide for their travel and living expenses it is estimated that tbe sum of $8,000 will be required. It is proposed to make a more frequent inspection of tbe Dominion lands and Crown timber offices, which will cost probably $1,000. Provision has been made for temporary help at agencies, should there be a rush of work, $2,500; expenses of inspector of agencies, $1,000; expenses of superintendent of mines, $1,000; contingencies of Dominion lands and Crown timber agencies, $14,000; printing and stationery. $0,000; express and freight charges, $700; legal expenses, $600; temporary help, $1,200; miscellaneous and unforeseen, $1,000.
Who is tbe commissioner of Dominion lands ?
Turriff.
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR J.   G.@

speechtext: Is he in the city now ?

No, he Is out west with one of the immigration agents of the department. He went about a week ago in company with an English journalist who is writing a series of letters in the English papers. Our immigration agent came across with him, and I sent Mr. Turriff along with him for the purpose of assisting him.
How many Dominion land agents are there and how many homestead inspectors ? How many perform the double duty of homestead inspector and Dominion lands agent ?

I am informed there is one homestead inspector in British Columbia, in the Kamloop district, who takes entries from settlers, but he is the only one. None of the other homestead inspectors are permitted to take entries.
Members of the hoard of examiners of Dominion land surveyors, including contingent expenses of board	 $300

On the previous item respecting surveys, I wished to ask a question, which I will ask now. I understand that representations were made to the department asking that further subdivisions Mr. CLANCY.
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR, The increase in the salaries, $7,000, is made up altogether by the appointment of temporary clerks at the head office. I need not read the names, but I have the list here. There are two subjects especially which have caused a very large amount of work in the department. One is the issuing of half-breed script in the North-west, which has entailed a large amount of clerical work; the other is the issuing of patents for the railway land grants. The amount of clerical work that has to be done in connection with both is very large. These clerks have been appointed only lately, and we are taking a supplementary estimate for the purpose of paying them for the balance of the present year. We will require to keep them on during the next year. They are all known as temporary writers. There are thirty-, two clerks. The total salaries will amount to $14,607.50; advertising, $2,302.50.
Protection of timber lands in Manitoba and the North-west Territories, and tree culture in the North-west Territories	 $15,000

This is an item as to which, I understand, there will be some discussion, not so much in regard to the item as in respect to the subject it refers to. Possibly this particular item might be allowed to stand for that purpose.
Yes, I would be very glad to leave that over.

Perhaps we may go on with the next one.
To provide for extra service in connection with Dominion lands, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil
Service Act	 $5,000
That covers, I think, somewhat the same service.

I am asking for this vote in connection with the preparation of patents for railway land grants. The department will have to have some special assistance other than the young ladies who are hired as temporary writers. We will probably have to have one or two men of some experience in work of that kind.
This item involves a very considerable question, as a new service is being entered upon in regard to the work of reforesting the country.
I have no objection in allowing the previous item to stand.
I take it that this item has no relation to the one provided for reforesting ?	.
No, none whatever.
I understand that the item respecting reforesting remains, and that the other item is adopted.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: The item of $15,000 remains.
Yes.
The only one we reserve is that for the protection of timber lands, &c.
The hon. Minister of the Interior has not stated what is the nature of the extra services that he requires..

This item has reference to the work of issuing patents for railway land grants. 1 have explained to my hon. friend that we will require some special assistance in connection with this other than that of those parties who are simply temporary writers. We will have to get, probably, the services of a solicitor, and possibly two, in order to check the work that is done by the others. We do not want to make permanent appointments, because this is not permanent work.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that that $17,000 is additional to this sum for extra services ?

1 am asking $5,000 separately, because there is a clause which says ' notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act.' The other appointments are made under the Civil Service Act.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. Do T understand that the hon. minister intends to employ clerks who are already employed by the government for their services ?

We will use the staff of the department to the' extent we can, and then we will have to secure some additional assistance. There will be no extra pay to any officers of the department.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. Then, why put in these words ' notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act.'

That will enable us to appoint a person at
more than $400 a year. We cannot appoint a person and pay more than $400 a year, as we have no authority to do so under the law. The law requires that we shall start a temporary writer at $400. We do not want to make permanent appointments, because this is not permanent work. We simply want to appoint temporary help.

Mr. Speaker, before the motion is put, I would like to mention to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) that the meeting of the Public Accounts Committee, which has been called for to-morrow, has been postponed. We are desirous, for the purpose of expediting the business of the House, that that committee should meet at once, and I understand from hon. gentlemen who are more familiar with the work of that committee than I am, that they desire that there should be at least two meetings each week. I am not, I think, a member of the committee myself, and, therefore, I am not familiar with its work, but that is what I understand from hon. gentlemen who are familiar with its work and who know what it will be called upon to do. I would like also to mention, on behalf of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), that the papers respecting the pay of ' C ' Battery have not been brought down. He desires that they should be brought down at an early date, so that they may be used for purposes connected with the estimates. I understand from the hon. Minister of Finance that we may look for the budget on Thursday.

Yes, the budget speech will be delivered on Thursday. In regard to the Public Accounts Committee, I may say that as the chairman of the Public Accounts Committee was out of town, I told my secretary, that if he could find whoever was acting in his place. I would be glad if it should be found convenient to postpone the meeting to-morrow, as I was anxious to be present. I received notice that the postponement had taken place. I may say. in regard to future meetings. that I do not anticipate there will be any difficulty after this week.
